Under MAR, issuers are required to disclose as soon as possible the inside information concerning them, to ensure that investors are informed and to prevent insider dealing. In specific circumstances, issuers may delay public disclosure to avoid prejudicing their legitimate interests. These guidelines help issuers in their decision to delay disclosure by providing a non-exhaustive list of legitimate interests that could justify such delay. title: ESMA updates its manual on transparency with new guidance for OTC derivatives and tick-size regime
summary: ESMA updates its manual on transparency with new guidance for OTC derivatives and tick-size regime 15 October 2026 Trading The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), the EU regulator and supervisor, has updated its manual on transparency to provide further guidance on the identification of over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives subject to transparency requirements and to enhance supervisory convergence on the application of the tick-size regime. The update also clarifies how the identifying reference data for OTC derivatives should be provided for transparency purposes, supporting greater consistency in the data reported to and published through the consolidated tape. The manual finally includes several published Q&As on the tick size regime, as well as the addition of recommendations on the application of the tick-size regime, comprising when trading venues and national competent authorities may intervene in specific circumstances. Next steps With regard to the guidance on OTC identifying reference data, the updated manual should be considered a draft until the entry into force of the related technical standards (RTS 2 and RTS on CTP input/output data). In 2025, national authorities across the EEA imposed more than 950 administrative sanctions and measures, a stable number compared with the past two years. The aggregated value of administrative fines amounted to almost €82 million. The report also highlights an increased use of settlements. As in previous years, activity remained focused mainly on breaches of the Market Abuse Regulation and the Markets in Financial Instruments Directive and Regulation. Enforcement activity remained concentrated in a small number of jurisdictions, with Germany, France and Spain accounting for two thirds of the total value of administrative fines across the EEA. title: ESMA analysis shows continued growth in cross-border investment services
summary: ESMA analysis shows continued growth in cross-border investment services 14 October 2026 Investor protection The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), the EU’s financial markets regulator and supervisor, has completed its annual analysis of the cross-border provision of investment services , together with national competent authorities (NCAs). The exercise collected data from investment firms across 30 jurisdictions in the EU/EEA and found that cross-border investment activity continued to grow significantly in 2025. Key findings: A total of 379 financial firms provided cross-border services to retail clients. Approximately 15.5 million clients in the EU/EEA received investment services from firms located in other Member States, almost twice as many as in 2023 . Compared to 2024 : The number of firms increased by 2%. The number of retail clients rose by 47%. Complaints remained stable (decreased by -0.2%). Cyprus remained the primary location for firms providing cross-border investment services in the EU/EEA, accounting for 20% of passporting firms, followed by Luxembourg (14%) and Germany (12%). In 2027, the Joint Committee will focus on areas where cooperation among the three ESAs is essential to support financial stability, consumer protection and effective supervision. Key priorities include digital operational resilience, technological innovation, sustainable finance, securitisation and cross-sectoral risk monitoring. Under the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA), the ESAs will continue oversight activities relating to critical ICT third-party service providers and work towards strengthening the financial sector’s preparedness against cyber threats. Market participants understand positive environmental or social impact differently and attach different levels of ambition to their impact claims.
